title: Graduate Student Performance Analysis: Study Hours vs. Exam Scores

child-questions.question:
A graduate business analytics course instructor analyzes student performance data to understand factors influencing exam scores. The scatter plot shows the relationship between study hours per week and final exam scores for 12 students. The data table provides additional metrics including prior GPA, course attendance, and assignment averages. Based on this data, answer the following questions:

1. Using the scatter plot, estimate the correlation coefficient between study hours and exam scores. What type of relationship does this suggest?
2. Calculate the average exam score for students who studied 20 hours or more per week, using the data table.
3. Identify which student (by ID) shows the greatest improvement from their assignment average to their exam score, and calculate this improvement percentage.
4. Determine if there is a threshold effect in study hours: at approximately how many study hours per week do exam scores begin to plateau (increase by less than 1% per additional hour)?
5. Considering all variables in the table, which factor appears most strongly associated with exam scores besides study hours, and provide a brief rationale based on the data trends.
child-questions.title: Multi-Factor Analysis of Graduate Student Performance Metrics

options.A: Strong positive correlation (r ≈ 0.95), suggesting more study hours lead to higher exam scores
options.B: Moderate positive correlation (r ≈ 0.75), indicating study hours moderately influence scores
options.C: Weak positive correlation (r ≈ 0.45), showing limited impact of study hours
options.D: No correlation (r ≈ 0), meaning study hours and exam scores are unrelated
options.E: Negative correlation (r ≈ -0.60), implying more study hours decrease scores

child-questions.solution:
{Improvement} = \frac{\text{Exam Score} - \text{Assignment Average}}{\text{Assignment Average}} \times 100\% \). For example, S001: (62-70)/70 × 100% = -11.43% (worse). S002: (68-75)/75 × 100% = -9.33%. S003: (75-78)/78 × 100% = -3.85%. S004: (82-82)/82 × 100% = 0%. S005: (85-85)/85 × 100% = 0%. S006: (88-88)/88 × 100% = 0%. S007: (90-90)/90 × 100% = 0%. S008: (92-92)/92 × 100% = 0%. S009: (94-94)/94 × 100% = 0%. S010: (95-95)/95 × 100% = 0%. S011: (96-96)/96 × 100% = 0%. S012: (97-97)/97 × 100% = 0%. All students have exam scores equal to or less than assignment averages, so no positive improvement. The greatest (least negative) is S003 with -3.85%.

Step 4: Determine the threshold where exam scores plateau (increase <1% per additional hour). Examine consecutive points: From 30 to 32 hours: score increases from 95 to 96 (1% increase). From 32 to 34 hours: 96 to 97 (1.04% increase). The increase is around 1% even at high hours, but looking earlier: 25 to 28 hours: 92 to 94 (2.17% over 3 hours ≈ 0.72% per hour). 28 to 30: 94 to 95 (1.06% over 2 hours ≈ 0.53% per hour). Plateau begins around 28-30 hours where per-hour increase drops below 1%.

Step 5: Identify the factor most strongly associated with exam scores besides study hours. Compare trends: Prior GPA increases with study hours and scores (e.g., from 3.2 to 4.0). Course attendance also increases (85% to 100%). Assignment averages closely match exam scores (differences small). Course attendance shows a near-perfect correlation with study hours and scores, especially at high values (100% attendance for top performers). Thus, course attendance appears most strongly associated, as it consistently aligns with performance.
